lesson.title: One Nation, One Broadcast: Radio and the Birth of Mass Media
lesson.summary: Radio broadcasting exploded in popularity during the 1920s, joining movies and mass circulation magazines to create, for the first time, a genuinely national culture that reached into homes across the country.
lesson.body:
Commercial radio broadcasting in the United States effectively began on November 2, 1920, when station KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast the results of the Harding Cox presidential election, one of the first live news broadcasts most Americans had ever heard. Within a few years radio went from a novelty to a fixture of American homes, fitting neatly into the same consumer culture that was filling houses with refrigerators and washing machines on credit. Families gathered around their radio sets in the evening the way earlier generations had gathered around the piano, listening to news, comedy, drama, and above all music.

The business of radio matured quickly. The National Broadcasting Company, or NBC, launched in 1926 as the first major national radio network, followed by the Columbia Broadcasting System, or CBS, in 1927. These networks linked local stations together so the same program could air simultaneously across the country, and they sold advertising to fund the broadcasts, extending the advertising driven model already reshaping print media into this new medium. For the first time, a listener in rural Kansas and a listener in New York City could hear the exact same voice, the exact same joke, and the exact same advertisement at the exact same moment, a genuinely new experience in American life.

Radio did not stand alone. Motion pictures, still silent for most of the decade, drew tens of millions of viewers to theaters each week, and the 1927 release of The Jazz Singer, the first feature film with synchronized dialogue, signaled the coming of talking pictures. Mass circulation magazines like Reader's Digest, founded in 1922, and Time, founded in 1923, packaged news and commentary for a national middle class audience. When aviator Charles Lindbergh completed the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight in May 1927, newspapers, newsreels, and radio broadcasts turned him into an instant national celebrity, a preview of how mass media would shape fame and public attention for the rest of the century. Together these new media technologies homogenized American culture in ways that print alone never had, spreading the same music, the same slang, and the same consumer desires from coast to coast.
